A dashboard shows a live clock above an expensive sales chart, and it stutters every second. The team does what every performance thread recommends: they move the clock's
into its own small widget so the dashboard stops rebuilding. A

It's easy to see where it comes from. "Rebuild" sounds like "redraw", and on the web "re-render" means updating what's on screen. Flutter's own docs tell you to avoid costly work in

local, which sounds like "rebuilds are expensive". And a rebuild can lead to a repaint, when it changes something visible. So "avoid rebuilds" is decent advice for the wrong reason, and it hides the other half: painting has its own triggers.
A frame runs in phases, and each one does only dirty work

Each frame goes through three phases that matter here: build, layout and paint. In the build phase, the framework keeps a list of dirty elements and jumps straight to them, skipping the clean ones. Layout visits only the
that need it and a limited area around them. Paint draws only the parts of the render tree that were marked as needing paint.
marks one element dirty for the build phase. Nothing in it says "paint this".
A rebuild that changes nothing paints nothing

When a widget rebuilds, each render object widget below it copies its new configuration onto its existing render object. The render object marks itself for layout or paint only when something it draws actually changed.

A repaint doesn't need a rebuild
docs say it plainly: a render object's

may be triggered even if its widgets didn't change or rebuild. A render object repaints whenever any render object that shares its layer is marked as needing paint: an ancestor scrolls, something animates, a text next to it changes. The mark travels up to the nearest
, possibly the root of the app, and painting that boundary repaints all of its descendants in the same layer. Animations often skip the build phase entirely: the Flutter docs note that a change to an
might trigger only the paint phase.
Not pixels. A rebuild costs CPU time on the UI thread: running your
methods, then walking the descendants until the walk meets an identical widget instance again. That's why the docs' advice stands: avoid repetitive and costly work in

as low in the tree as you can; push state to the leaves; use
. Notice what none of that controls: how much gets painted.

blocks.title: A RepaintBoundary everywhere is not a fix

content.text: Each boundary gives its subtree a layer of its own. That only pays off when the child and its parent paint at different times; when they paint together, the API docs say the boundary is redundant and may make performance worse. Scrolling lists already wrap each item in one by default (
), and their docs note that for children that are cheap to paint, such as a short text, skipping the boundary can be more efficient.

content.text: How to apply it in your project

items.title: Measure the phase that's actually slow

content.text: Profile in profile mode with the DevTools Performance view. Its Track Widget Builds option shows
events in the timeline, and Track Paints shows paint events. They add overhead themselves, so turn them on only while you investigate.
Move parsing, sorting and heavy formatting out of
and into state that changes only when the data does. A
that only assembles widgets can run often without hurting anyone.
Give a fast-changing value its own small widget, as the docs suggest with a dedicated clock widget. Use
where you can, and pass subtrees that don't change as a
instead of rebuilding them inside a builder.

items.title: Contain repaints where painting is expensive

content.text: Wrap content that's costly to paint and rarely changes, like a chart, a map or a complex illustration, when it sits next to something that repaints often. Then check the boundary's metrics, and remove it if it isn't useful.
